utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Sorry to commence with something as mundane as scheduling concerns but I thought it best to raise them now. I had discussed them briefly with Mr. Robinson earlier. So, a few matters arise that I wanted to bring to the Court's attention, and hopefully with some anticipation, we might be able to resolve them. First of all, the Court will recall perhaps that the testimony of Mr. Banbury was rescheduled from commencing on 14th to 15th and discussions about his interview by the accused also took place with the Defence and while -- and now on the basis of the understanding that we would not be sitting on the 14th, which was the reason for moving him to the 15th, in the first place. Now I understand we are scheduled for the -- to have court on the 14th. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Are we scheduled to sit on 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what I understood from the Registry yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is so scheduled, but the Chamber is not in the position to sit on the 14th. That's why I -- probably that message has not been -- has not been conveyed clearly to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see, Mr. President. Well, that certainly obviates one problem so I'm pleased that we raised it. In a related matter, we are trying to project out the appearances of witnesses for a number of reasons, one of which is whether or not we would come to the commencement of proceedings and have witnesses left who didn't testify. I discussed that with Mr. Robinson as well. Another is whether or not witnesses would have to give way for long periods to fixed witnesses. So in that regard I would ask two things. Number 1, if the Court would be in a position to provide the cross-examination estimates for KDZ182 and Mr. Banbury at the earliest opportunity; and number 2, if there was the possibility of exploring whether or not some extended sessions could be held perhaps tomorrow and/or Tuesday of next week, and that might eliminate the risk of one of the witnesses being here for quite an extended time waiting while fixed witnesses take the stand. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will consider the matters. Unless there are other matters to be raised, we will bring in the witness, Mr. Muracevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One additional inquiry, the current court calendar, as you noted, erroneously has us sitting on the 14th but it also notes that we are not sitting on the 18th, and I didn't know if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will move Tuesday to Friday. Good morning, Mr. Muracevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, time is precious, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Excellency Lattanzi. I am glad to see you back. That means that you have recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Muracevic, how are you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very well, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we went a little bit forward with respect to the events. Therefore let's go back in time. A critical time in Svrake. And up until the 2nd of May, you practically had no war. There was only tension and mutual mistrust; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that. Concerning the departure of Serbs from our village, it wasn't related only to the need to have peaceful nights outside our village, but overnight there was shooting from the places where they went, from automatic weapons, and that caused anxiety in the village where I was living.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was fire opened at your village, Mr. Muracevic, or was that just the shooting into the air?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some shooting into the air but at times a stray bullet would reach our village as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anyone hurt?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in those shootings prior to the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us be accurate. I put it to you that that many Serbs, 170 of them, in the midst of 1080 Muslims needed to go to other villages to spend nights in uncomfortable conditions because they were afraid and they were frightened of your guards, not in order to shoot at your village.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Karadzic. People from our village, who lived in the centre part of the village, had their houses on the edges of the village. Therefore, they did not sleep in uncomfortable conditions. They slept in their own houses, because many of them, on the slopes of the Paljevo hill, had built houses later in the centre of the village, such as the Cetkovic family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you closely connected and did you have close cooperation with your police station?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Since our police station had a branch office, so to speak, in our local commune, we can say that we were keeping close relationship because part of the police force from Vogosca was deployed in my local commune, and I'm talking about the part of the reserve police force, that they were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am making a pause, and you should know why I'm doing that, and please also pause before answering. These two telegrams of the 12th and the 29th of April, did they contain information about the attack on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have -- need to look at these telegrams but I don't think that anyone from the police notified me of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw this document yesterday but we can look at it again. I think it's -- but let me check the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could D400 be shown to the witness in order to refresh his memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the second one, immediately prior to your crisis. D400.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Press e-court.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an opportunity to see this document before the conflict broke out in my village. As I said yesterday, I saw this document for the first time here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the date, which is the 29th of April? And it says to the Security Services Centres, all of them, SJB, all of them, and secretary of the Sarajevo SUP, and then it says, "Order on the implementation of the decision of the Presidency of the Republic BH," and then this is followed by the number of the order. And it says, "On the 27th of April, the decision was made," and then, under number 1: "It is ordered to carry out the full and massive blockade of all road intersections on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on which the units of the former JNA are beginning to withdraw technical and material assets and do that in coordination with the MUP. Carry out the blockade of the wider region of military facilities from which technical and material assets are attempted to be taken out of with various methods of formational and natural barriers which should be secured for the units of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of BH. Unannounced convoys of units of the former JNA and those that are not escorted by the MUP should be prevented from leaving the barracks and communicating on the territory of the Republic of BH. Immediately begin preparing and initiating battle activities on the entire territory of the Republic of BH and coordinate them with the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of the region, district or Republic of BH. Within the scope of battle activities, plan all encompassing measures of protecting the population, the material assets of the citizens of the Republic of BH. Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic." Therefore there is no doubt that your police station had received this. Why didn't they inform you about these preparations for war operations against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: There were elements of the police in my village, so I can tell you with full responsibility, and I said that yesterday as well, I saw this document for the first time yesterday. Before the conflict broke out in my local commune, nobody told me about the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to believe you but do you think that it would be appropriate for the secretary of the local commune to be notified about what was being prepared at the Semizovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some police actions regarding the barracks in Semizovac, but there was no need, actually, for that because the army had already distributed the weapons from Semizovac to the local Serbs a long time before that. Nobody informed me about this but they should have done that, and as I said yesterday, I knew nothing about this document, and I saw it for the first time here in the courtroom. But I didn't know about this document, nor did anyone inform me about the content of this document before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that in testimony of yours, which is in document 1D3349, in your testimony in the case versus Dragan Damjanovic, before the state court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when asked whether you attacked by the JNA, you said, "No, it was done by our Serb neighbours who were stationed within the JNA facilities." Let me ask you this for starters: Do you agree that the Slovenes, the Croats, the Muslims, failed to respond to the call-up of the reserve forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some of them didn't. However, as far as the activities of the local Serbs and the JNA is concerned with relation to the Semizovac barracks, I can state with full responsibility that the local Serbs enjoyed tremendous support by the JNA stationed at the Semizovac barracks, which, until 1991, until the conflict broke out, was gradually coming under the control of the Serbian authorities. So in a way, the Semizovac barracks served as a kind of compound where weapons were being distributed, where local Serbs were trained in handling the weapons, and also when all these barricades were erected, it provided a significant logistical support to the local Serbs by placing all the JNA assets in the Semizovac barracks at their disposal. So the local Serbs and members of the JNA who were at the Semizovac barracks acted in concert against my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's turn this a little bit upside down. I put it to you not that the local Serbs had the support of the local Serbs but that it was vice versa and that it was only the local Serbs who responded to the call-up, but the Muslims and the Croats didn't.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I was not part of the JNA structure. I had no opportunity to see what was the rate of response to the mobilisation. What I'm telling you is based on my own experience as the secretary of the local commune because my local commune had an excellent cooperation with Pero Crnogorac, the commander of the barracks, and the barracks itself, in terms of cultural cooperation and every other cooperation, and also previously through TO units that were joint, and we always had understanding on the part of the Semizovac barracks before the war. Therefore, there was no need for the people at the barracks to be frightened of the villagers of Svrake because, for years before that, the population did not show in any way whatsoever that they were bent on threatening the safety and security of the soldiers. After all, the JNA was the army of our common country and state, and we considered it to be our army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that until the 2nd of May, 1992, the JNA had already had bloody and terrifying experiences with their barracks in Slovenia and Croatia, where they were under blockade, where soldiers were killed, where they had electricity, water and telephone lines cut off, that it had been humiliated and that as a whole it was under the threat posed by the local population in those republics?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: From the media, I know what was going on, but the Semizovac barracks did not face these problems. As a commander of the barracks, he was my friend. Dobrica Stojanovic was also there. We were good friends. And as secretary of the local commune and representatives of my local commune and representatives of the executive branch in those times when these events were taking place in Slovenia and Croatia, we went to the barracks to pay them visits, to exchange experiences, to discuss the shooting that was happening overnight around our villages, and we asked the JNA to help us calm down the situation and try to reduce the level of the shooting that was present at the time. In other words, there was no fear that the local Muslims in my local communes would threaten the safety and security of the JNA barracks in Semizovac in any way whatsoever, and their commander Pero Crnogorac and other associates of his, on the other hand, never warned us, as something that might due to our conduct jeopardise their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please focus on your answers because I don't think that you would like to stay here tomorrow as well, but nevertheless, we would like to hear everything that you wish to say. Now, if I put it to you that the Semizovac barracks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The previous question put by Mr. Karadzic to the witness was about Slovenia and Croatia and I was about to rise and ask him what the relevance of that question was in any event. And now he's telling the witness to focus when, in fact, he was the one that put the question. And the witness actually brought it back to his commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may just say that the relevance is in the fact that the army already had such experiences and they had reasons to be afraid, and since they intercepted these two telegrams, and I had them on my desk on the same day the Muslims sent me those telegrams, so they also knew about them. So if I were to ask you, Mr. Muracevic, if you agreed that the Semizovac barracks was mostly for the warehousing of ammunition and fuel for the JNA, would you say "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the JNA barracks in Semizovac and the one in Misoca was one of the barracks used to store fuel, lubricants and so on. So it was more of a depot, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D3349? I don't see -- I don't see it. I don't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript from your testimony in the Damjanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Your Honour, this is actually a summary of the witness's testimony. Mr. Karadzic has the witness's full testimony at 1D03350, so I think it's better to take the witness to his actual testimony and not a summary of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Summary of his transcript or the excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. The document Mr. Karadzic is taking the witness to now is a summary of the transcript of his evidence, but we do have the witness's actual evidence at 1D03350, and I think if Mr. Karadzic is going to put any questions to the witness, he should put his actual testimony to him and not the summary of the transcript of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with Ms. Sutherland's observation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we then get that number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next -- just next 65 ter number. 1D3350. You have it in your list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's there but in order to save time, it would have been easier for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in response to the question that -- were you attacked by the JNA, you replied at these proceedings, during the cross-examination, your reply to lawyer Stojanovic, that it was not the JNA but that it was the neighbours, the local Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: We were attacked in coordination by local Serbs and the members of the Yugoslav People's Army who were there because the local Serbs were -- a large number of them were billeted at the Semizovac barracks any way. So in a way when I say "the local Serbs" that already would imply that it was the local Serbs who had been well instructed by that time and already billeted at the barracks in Semizovac. So in some way the attack of the local Serbs on my village was in full coordination with the equipment and materiel located at the Semizovac barracks. Fire was opened from Semizovac itself and also from the actual facility of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you still said it wasn't the JNA but it was the Serb neighbours. I kindly ask for a little bit of patience. I thought that this summary would help to us work more quickly. Now we are going to get the right page. It's page 33 in the Serbian. Up there, your answers at the top: "Stojanovic, no, not the JNA but our neighbours, the Serbs from Semizovac, Krivoglavci, and the inhabitant Serbs from Svrake, meaning that they used the capacities of the former Yugoslav People's Army, specifically the barracks in Semizovac, which up until then was a barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, even the air force?" Were the peasants from Krivoglavci and Semizovac have aviation [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the villages, the peasants, did they have the aviation, you may say that they didn't but a member of the Serbian ethnic group from my village was a pilot from the Yugoslav People's Army, and during the attack, the air force of the JNA was used on my village and, specifically, a number of buildings were damaged in the bombardment and some of the air bombs that were dropped on my village did not activate. And then later, the local Serbs, when the village fell, took some of those unexploded air bombs and took them to certain housing facilities, public and private ones, and blew up those buildings. Specifically in that way they knocked down my home, the local mosque in Svrake and they also blew up a commercial building in another local commune. Part of this testimony from this court does say that we were attacked by the local Serbs who, to their full capacity, used all that the JNA had at its disposal in the Semizovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on something, please? Can we make it a little bit more succinct? Mr. Muracevic, did you know that pilot from your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. His name was Predrag Cetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he deployed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was deployed, but before the conflict broke out, I had the opportunity to see him once when he landed in a helicopter at the local stadium in my local commune. I had the opportunity then to see him myself as he was getting out of the helicopter. He wasn't operating an aeroplane at the time but he had at that time come to visit his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. But you don't know whether he took part in this action or not?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm that. From the ground you cannot see who is piloting the airplanes, and it wasn't just one plane in the action but several. So if he was one of the pilots, this is something that I couldn't have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So let's clarify this, then. Was this action by the air force the action by the JNA or some private action of one of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the air force began to operate, actually I'm not aware that any private individual had a war plane that was part of the JNA formations in his own private possession. Several aeroplanes that bombed my village, though, were planes of the Yugoslav People's Army. They were part of their arsenal. I'm not aware that any individual could have had such a type of combat plane in their personal possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the mosque was damaged in a subsequent action by an unexploded bomb or was it hit by an aeroplane?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in Svrake was significantly damaged after an air bomb that had not exploded was activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So it wasn't struck by an air bomb, was it?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you understand, the minaret of that mosque was not destroyed during that attack on our village but it was destroyed later when an unexploded air bomb was detonated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many people were killed in that action, from the 2nd to the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: One person was killed and four people were wounded in my settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the amalgamated statement, paragraph -- let me just tell you which one, you say that a number of people were killed. Why do your more recent statements paint the Serbs in a worse light?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please show me that statement? As far as I know, I always said that one person was killed and four were wounded. Perhaps this was something to the effect that several people were hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 13 of your amalgamated statement now, please? Here it says: "[In English] People were wounded and killed. [Interpretation] One person was killed and the second one killed themselves?" Well, it arises from this that people were wounded and killed. How is it that you increase the number in this general formulation when one person was killed?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're evidently either not reading what I said. One person was killed and that means that one person was killed in that period. At that point in time, it wasn't possible to determine whether that person was killed from a self-inflicted wound or from fire from somebody else. So one person was killed, four people were wounded. In the statement at the time, we couldn't pinpoint whether that person was killed by fire from the Serbs or as a result of a self-inflicted wound. So one person was killed, four were wounded. There are no two persons killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it says people were wounded and killed. Can you please tell us how that one person was killed?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when the person was hurt, but the person had a wound. I was able to get to that person, to their house, and I could see a specific wound in the chest. Since, in the action on my village, different kinds of ammunition were used, fragmentation ammunition and dumdum bullets, I couldn't really tell whether the person was really hit by fire from local Serbs or perhaps by a weapon that that person happened to have on them. So in the statement it is not precisely stated whether the person was killed as a result of fire from Serbs or as a result of self-wounding. I wasn't able to establish how the person died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, believe me, all of that can be said much, much more briefly.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's up to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say that at that point in time, you didn't know whether the person was killed by their own device or they were hit by some Serbs. Did you know that when you gave the consolidated statement? Was it clarified that that person died from a wound inflicted from their own home-made pistol?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to see that later. When the person was actually killed, no criminal investigation was carried out to establish the cause of death. The body was there unburied for days and then, after a few days, it was buried at the local cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I didn't ask you where and when the person was buried. Can we please look at 3354? Is your memory better today than it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for my specific recollection of this particular event, I couldn't establish whether the person was killed by Serb soldiers or by a self-inflicted wound from the weapon that he had on him. I stuck more by the option that he was probably killed from a self-inflicted wound, and that was the context even though there was no particular investigation. This was more a matter of my personal conviction than an actual --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Sir, you escaped on the 5th of December, and then on the 6th, you provided your first statement, "yes" or "no"? We can go with a "yes" or "no" here, please.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 3 of this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are looking at page 1 but can we look at page 3 in the Serbian? I believe that it's probably page 3 in the English as well. Can we please look at the first paragraph of page 3 of this statement? Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the statement, I stuck to the option that the person was killed from a self-inflicted wound because the person had an improvised device on them which could have caused the wound. So in that context, I stayed by the option that it was actually self wounding and not perhaps a shot fired by the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see what you say in the beginning. You say: "I went towards the bus station in Vogosca where I managed to get to Semizovac in a bus of Centrotrans, by hiding myself, where I increased the combat readiness of the TO units and the reserve police, and called on the population to undertake maximum measures of caution and use of shelters" and so on and so forth. So you managed to raise the combat readiness of the units. Why did you do that, Mr. Muracevic?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: From what you read, you can see why. Had I not done that, had I not taken the inhabitants to a safe place, I assumed that there would have been many more casualties in my village than there already were, because for days before that you could hear the rattling of weapons around our village, especially from early 1992. So in some way we were constantly afraid of some possible attack occurring. An attack was even attempted between the 3rd and 4th of April, 1992, because in the Krivoglavci local community there was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Please believe me --

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but, Mr. Karadzic, Your Honours, if I can clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Muracevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For months before the attack on my village, the neighbouring village and the local commune of Krivoglavci, where the firing range of the JNA was, as well as of the TO and everybody else, that's where they checked weapons. For days, on that firing range, local Serbs, together with various volunteers who arrived from theatres of war in Slovenia, Croatia, stayed there. One day, between the 3rd and 4th of April, 1992, from this road between Zenica, Sarajevo, where there was a police station right by Krivoglavci, they tried to attack my village from there. They even opened fire. But thanks to the night guards we had, they didn't manage to enter the village. So in a way, before the 2nd of May when my village was attacked, it had gone on for months, gunfire provocations, everything that happened at the firing range in Krivoglavci, all these people who we hadn't known before who came to this firing range and who tested different weapons. We were afraid, in a way, and we were waiting for something to happen to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, as for these incidents and attacks against your village before the 2nd of May, you never said a word of any of that in your previous statements, right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Perhaps you did not have an opportunity to read all the statements that are referred to in the footnotes. But when we spoke about the Serb population getting out of our village and the beginning of 1992, when in my statements I refer to armed Serb guards around our village, also the trenches that were dug out around our village, that in a way went without saying, what was possibly in the making as far as my local commune was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, going without saying is not a fact. It is a fact that you never stated that any Serb had attacked you before the 2nd of May. Do show us a statement where you said that, or tell us of a criminal complaint that was filed before that. However, let's deal with this now. Sacir Fejzovic, you did know that on the 6th of December, was killed as the result of a self-inflicted wound, and when you were compiling your amalgamated statement you said that people were wounded and killed. Tell us now, is that what you said or did this sort of slip into your statement?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't slip into my statement. It is a fact that Sacir Fejzovic was killed during the attack on my village. Now, was this deadly wound self-inflicted or was it inflicted by the Serbs, there is nothing special in that respect. It is a fact that he lost his life in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Mr. Karadzic knows well, the witness doesn't prepare the amalgamated witness statements, the Office of the Prosecutor does based on all of the witness's prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he read through --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He reviewed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- reviewed and confirmed --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He reviewed the amalgamated statement but he's not the one that puts the amalgamated statement together, if I can put it like that. And also, in relation to paragraph 9, if Mr. Karadzic reads when he -- the witness actually does say that there was a lot of firing and they sometimes turned the weapons on the Svrake village. So that sort of information is contained already in the witness's statement, also in relation to the sentence "People were wounded and killed," the footnote to that specific sentence takes Mr. Karadzic to the witness's prior statement where he says, four people were wounded and one was killed. And that was a statement taken in 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect to Ms. Sutherland, we object to the amalgamated statements because they were authored by the OTP. As we move on, they get worse and worse, as far as the Serbs are concerned. And on the 6th of December, 1992, this witness unequivocally stated that Sacir Fejzovic killed himself with this device that he had made by himself. So as time goes by, and as the OTP creates more and more of these statements, the Serbs look worse and worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With respect to the amalgamated statements, Your Honour, the OTP has been instructed by the Trial Chamber to prepare an amalgamated witness statement or submit one testimony of a witness. This witness has not testified previously before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the population had been warned by the JNA as well to seek shelter and to take care of themselves because there would be operations under way?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The population of Svrake had not been warned by the JNA that there would be certain operations under way. That is to say that the population of my village had not been informed by the JNA that there would be certain operations under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then who spoke to the population through a loud speaker and warned them to hand over their weapons, telling them that there would be operations going on?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was done by the local Serbs. The local Serbs. They used a loud speaker, issuing warnings. There were all sorts of threats issued as well. At any rate, the local Serbs were calling upon people to leave the village. In these threats they did not say that it would be the JNA that would attack or whoever. They were just calling upon the population to leave the village. And as for the people themselves, why would they leave their homes of their own accord, just like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see that -- or, rather, let us see what you said in 1D3350.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that back? Can we have the next page? Next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that two of your representatives went to negotiate and received guarantees that they could leave and they did leave with one group, and another group was left behind and that group was taken to the barracks, right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about that yesterday. It's not two groups. It is one and the same group. The local Serbs and members of different armies cut it off. There was just this one group, this one column, that was cut off by the local Serbs, the army and all sorts of other formations that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday we saw that that was not the case, that they did not inform you and that you left in a great rush only after them, and that that is why you were not included in this announcement that pertained to the first group. So you were warned through loudspeakers that the population could seek shelter while operations were under way, right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right, Mr. Karadzic. Now you are misstating what we discussed yesterday. We did not discuss that yesterday. These two gentlemen who went to negotiate with the local Serbs, familiarised me with the agreements that had been reached. However, the two of them did not familiarise the entire village with that. However, I went, together with my co-workers, to warn the rest of the people in the village about this, and to tell them that we should leave the village in an organised manner. It is a fact that these two and part of the column left before the set deadline. That is to say, before the entire village managed to get together at this point of departure. So this column that they started was one column. And it was just cut off, and part of that column was taken to the Semizovac barracks. There was no mention whatsoever of one column leaving and another one having who knows what happen to it. It was the entire population of the village that was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what happened exactly in the barracks. There were about 400 people there, right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next day, after the night was spent within the barracks compound, women, children, the elderly, civilians, were returned into the village.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I was among the first to be taken out of the barracks, and I found out only a few days later that women and children were taken back to the village and that men from the barracks in Semizovac were taken to Naka's garage, close to the Vogosca flyover, and after that, they were returned to Svrake, but they were supposed to report to Planjo's house. Later on, it turned into everyday detention for them. 28 villagers from my village were taken in an unknown direction, sometime in mid-June, from that particular location, and to this day, no one knows what happened to these 28 persons except for three of them whose mortal remains we found after the war in the bed of the Bosna River near Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, that is part of one of my next questions. We'll get to that. That is a very important thing. So were you with these people who were in Naka's garage, and did you spend 33 days there, or were you taken further immediately?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I was immediately taken to the bunker, but on one occasion they took me from Naka's garage, where I spent one night, and almost half of the next day. Actually, on one particular day, they took me from the bunker to Naka's garage. I spent the night there. So I had the opportunity of seeing that in this facility of Naka's garage, there were 150, or perhaps even more than 150, villagers from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So nine of you were detained in the bunker. You mention or you accepted that the Serbs knew what you had been doing. Today we read that you were the person who raised combat readiness there. Yesterday, we saw, from your very own words, that you smuggled a mortar and mortar rounds. However, you said that among these nine, there were some for whom you did not know why they had been detained in the bunker. Are you trying to say that there was some personal revenge involved there, because one of them was a teacher and then one of his students was after him? Could you try to deal with this as briefly as possible? If it wasn't the case of personal revenge in your personal case, because you were involved in preparing the defence, what about all these other people?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic puts about four or five statements and then says try and deal with this as briefly as possible and then goes on again. So he needs to put a question and get an answer, and a question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about time, Mr. Karadzic, to -- for your skills to have improved. One by one, and be simple in putting questions. But can you answer the question or shall I ask the accused to reformulate his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since Mr. Karadzic said a few things that were untrue in relation to what I did, I wish to say that I did not smuggle a mortar. We took it away from the local Serbs at the check-point. How come they had it? I did not smuggle anything. Smuggling means that you are buying and reselling things for personal profit. As for the specific question, whether there was any personal revenge involved, in this group of nine men from Svrake, there weren't any teachers who were there with me. Obviously the teacher that he is actually referring to is the man who was brought in much later, not together with these nine men from Svrake. But I would not say that it was a question of personal revenge or anything like that. Quite simply, it was something coordinated that was done by the local Serbs. For instance, before my village was attacked, Jovan Tintor, as the leader of the local organisation of the Serb Democratic Party and president of the Crisis Staff, almost a day before my village was attacked issued an order in relation to the Kontiki bed and breakfast, that is better known as Kod Sonja. He declared it to be his staff. And that is what they had intended to do, that they would bring certain people detained in there, in the bunker, and it so happened that I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let me tell you something. A moment ago I recapitulated what you said yesterday, that, yes, you were smuggling, but I mean it wasn't smuggling for the sake of selling something. You managed to get a mortar into the town of Sarajevo through Serb lines, surreptitiously and also a few mortar rounds. And now you mentioned Jovan Tintor. Do you agree or should we look for a document, that Jovan Tintor only had this building handed over to the Ministry of Justice and that the prison was something that the Ministry of Justice planned, not Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the facilities that were used for detaining the non-Serb population, they could be subdivided, as it were. Jovan Tintor, as the president of the local organisation of the SDS in Vogosca and president of the Crisis Staff, did have influence over the local authorities, the establishment of local authorities --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, please. This is a very restricted question. You mentioned that Jovan Tintor decided to detain people and that he intended to use Planjo's house for those purposes and that he designated it for that. Jovan Tintor, as a local functionary, approved that it be handed over to the Ministry of Justice. Was Planjo's house under the Ministry of Justice, the department for sanctions, and for keeping captives and detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are constantly trying to put words in my mouth. I said that by his order, Mr. Jovo Tintor placed Kontiki and the bunker as the facilities for detention. As for Planjo's house, it had been a detention facility throughout the whole period. I think that sometime in mid-July 1992, the local authorities issued an order, and by this order, it was placed at the disposal of the Ministry of the Interior. And even before that order, Planjo's house was used to detain people from Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D3351. On the 6th of December, it was quite clear to you how Sacir was killed, and then on the 26th of December -- can we have the next page, it's 1D3351. This is your statement from 1992, can we look at page 3? The first complete sentence reads: "As a result of this operation, Sacir Fejzovic was killed, son of Smajo, and four people were wounded." On the previous page it says that the JNA bombed Svrake with two aircraft, and that Sacir Fejzovic was killed as a result. Only two weeks later, you have completely twisted this whole story and attributed this to the Serbs. Why did you you do that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that Sacir Fejzovic was killed during these war operations. In my previous statement I only clarified it to the effect that I wasn't sure whether he was killed by a bullet from the Serbs or whether he died of a self-inflicted wound. So I wasn't determining anything. I just wanted to state the fact that one person was killed and four were wounded. And I don't see anything that is in dispute here, because there is a possibility here that this was a self-inflicted wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on this page, where Hajrudin Djulovic is mentioned and Senad Kevla [phoen] reached an agreement but failed to inform the population, but rather, on the 5th of May, people set off in a disorganised way so that the enemy forces let a small portion of the population to pass through. So we are finished with this. Now, when you were in the bunker, are you talking about the bunker next to Sonja's restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this facility fenced?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the bunker itself or the entire facility of Kontiki guest house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where you stayed, were this whole compound secured by a fence?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: On the side facing the local road, I think there was a -- there was a hedge, and there were guards posted by the prison management. So on the side facing the road that connected Semizovac and Vogosca was a kind of hedge, maybe there was also a fence there, but I'm not quite sure. It might have been concealed by this greenery. And there was a gate leading into the compound, whereas on the other side, where the railroad tracks were, there was no fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a hedge needs time to grow up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know how it looked before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was no wire fence, and when you went out you were not confined in a wired area?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were going out from the bunker, there was no wired or mesh fence, but the whole compound was fenced, or rather, restricted from one side by the railroad and the other side by the hedge next to the road. So that constituted a kind of physical barrier in which there was a gate leading to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in time, the Serbs brought mattresses from the gym for you to sleep on them, and these became soaked later by rain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the inmates had been roasting lambs on stakes whenever delegations came to visit them, for example, UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The bunker inmates were taken out quite often to perform a kind of -- all kinds of jobs, including roasting lambs when some celebrations were held, and that included the visit by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between the answer and your question. You make the life of Judge Lattanzi, who has just recovered, very difficult. The French interpreters are relying on the English translation, so you have to further slow down. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One more reason for me to make an effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some detainees would go to the well to fetch water and that they picked pears on the way?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that some detainees were taken to the well which was in close proximity to the Kontiki guest house. Now, whether they picked pears on the way, I suppose they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they being taken there or were they being sent to the well to fetch the water?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken from the bunker, but I don't know whether from the Kontiki, they were let go to go there on their own. However, I saw quite often that these detainees were accompanied by guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But sometimes it happened that they had no escort but that you were, rather, sent away to the well to bring water and that on the way they would pick pears and bring them back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, yesterday you spoke about various interpretations and translations. When we say that people were taken out of the bunker to carry out jobs, including the fetching of water, I could not have known whether they were taken from the Kontiki guest house and whether they were escorted by the guards. But I think in most cases, they were accompanied by the guards who were providing security for the Kontiki and the detention facility as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you tell your people, after you escaped, that you had seen and identified General MacKenzie, when he came to visit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a statement given before representatives of UNPROFOR or the international community, I explained under which circumstances I saw General MacKenzie. However, after I left prison, and in the context of the statements that I gave at the time, I mentioned in passing visits paid by representatives of the international community, specifically UNPROFOR. However, in it my statements given in early 1993, I wasn't able to confirm that in the context relating to the account of the visit of UNPROFOR to this facility, that were given by some other detainees, or members of the Serbian army, such as Borislav Herak and Sretko Damjanovic, as well as some of the inmates of the bunker who had often been taken to do the roasting of lambs, so in my statements given in early 1993, it was not possible for me to confirm, based on their stories, the fact that I saw UNPROFOR coming to the area. All I knew was what I heard from these inmates who told me that they had come to that area. Sometime towards the end of 1994, I subsequently recalled a situation when a Serbian soldier whom I hadn't known before, because he was not part of the security detail in the prison, who came to take me out of the bunker and take me in an unknown direction. Because he was treating me in that way, I had an opportunity to see in front of the very restaurant certain UNPROFOR vehicles. I did not link this event at the time with UNPROFOR visits to this location irrespective of the fact that, for days before that, the prison management were speaking about a visit by members -- representatives of the international community and General MacKenzie. I just was aware of this kind of situation and I heard guards saying that Mr. Tintor had appropriated or misappropriated in a certain way a number of UNPROFOR vehicles. I thought that that was the situation in which they would use one such vehicle to transport me to Pale or somewhere else. Now, in those circumstances, I noticed a number of people dressed in UNPROFOR uniforms, and among them, I noticed an individual about whom I was not aware at the time that that was General MacKenzie. I learned that only much later when I saw on TV. It reminded me that it was possible that general himself was there in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will kindly have to ask the Chamber to give me some time tomorrow as well because you are giving me really lengthy answer. Now, is it true that in the BH media, a campaign was launched against General MacKenzie in which there were allegations that the Serbs pimped minor Muslim girls to him at the restaurant? Do you remember that campaign?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that people were making statements to that effect, and the possibility that something like that happened. However, I was in Kontiki, and I knew that representatives of the international community came to visit us and I know that on such occasions, lambs were roasted and all these feasts were prepared, but I couldn't know any specifics about what this was all about. There were situations like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just stick to "yes" or "no"? After your escape, did you state that you had seen and recognised General MacKenzie, and that at the time, there were four girls loosely dressed and that it you couldn't believe that that was attributable to such a reputable general?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not involved in these intrigues targeting General MacKenzie because this visit of his to Kontiki was being discussed by the Serbs, such as Borislav Herak and Sretko Damjanovic, who were detained alongside me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want to confirm that Borislav Herak and Srecko Damjanovic were convicted by the Bosnia-Herzegovinian court of murder of people who later on turned out to be alive; "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite familiar with the grounds on which they were convicted. I know that one of the persons charged, whether Sretko Damjanovic or the other one, one of the victims appeared to be alive and his sentence was reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or he was maybe acquitted because it was decided that everything was fabricated and based on lies?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't -- Sretko Damjanovic wasn't acquitted. He was sentenced to eight years in prison and the time spent in prison during trial was credited to his total sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a human shield? Were you used as human shield once?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you taken out of the bunker to perform labour?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D3356? How many times were you taken out for work assignments from the bunker?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken from the bunker twice, but throughout the whole period of my detention, I was taken out six times tops, but specifically twice from the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you see that this is an interview that you gave to Lars Nielsen in 1994, a police inspector of the United Nations? Do you remember that he interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that they talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told him that you escaped on the 5th of December, after being used as a human shield, live shield. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now get -- just one moment, please. Could all the participants please take a look at this first page before we move to the next one? It states here -- I will have to read in English here: "[In English] The witness explained that there was no well situated on the plot. He knew, however, that there was a well somewhere east of the plot. He knew that the well was located near the pear tree. He knew this because when people had been sent for water, they often brought back pears. Most of the time it was Hido, Ahmed, and Zornic, Zlatan, who were sent to the well." [Interpretation] And then on page 2 it says that there was no fence on the northern side of the restaurant, that the parking lot was on the eastern side, and that there was a green fence, a hedge, you have said that, and that there was no barbed wire fence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say a little bit further along: [In English] "At the end of May 1992, beginning of June 1992, the prison held about 40 male prisoners. These were held in the bunker, together with one woman. In the barracks were held four girls from the village Vogosca. He did not know them by name but he recognised their faces. He assumed that they were Muslims." [Interpretation] Were they waitresses or were they something else? Because you say here, "He assumed" so you assumed something; is that right? Did you know were they waitresses or were they something else?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Those girls were not waitresses in that location, and since during those days I was frequently taken out to a hut that was between the bunker and the Kontiki guest house, I had the opportunity to see those girls. I had the opportunity even to hear when the prison warden, Branko Vlaco, was giving certain instructions to the girls, how they would behave towards the guests. I didn't know which guests were in question at the time, but judging by their expression I could see that these were persons there who had been brought from outside of the locality of the territory of the Kontiki guest house, and they were not part of the restaurant staff at the guest house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that men and women detainees were permitted to go out, but at the time they were accompanied by armed guards? Are you -- then you speak here about how you got these mats. Can we look at page 3. Can you please tell us how you identified General MacKenzie, and you talk about it on this page? What did you notice about him that made you convinced that it was him?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's described there. I don't have anything particular to add other than just something that is not indicated in the statement. I don't know because it's an English translation so I don't know exactly what is written there, but I think that that person that I later identified as General MacKenzie had an unusual watch on his wrist. It was a bit larger than what I had had the opportunity to see, in terms of watch size before. But everything else is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "MacKenzie was dressed in green battle dress. [In English] His shirt sleeves were rolled up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a copy of the statement that's been translated into B/C/S if it -- to assist the witness. This was disclosed to the Defence a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not yet uploaded in the e-court? Yes, a hard copy can be provided to the witness. Shall we take a break, Mr. Karadzic, now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Trial Chamber, in view of these very long answers, allow me a bit more time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more would you need? You have half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least the next session. The witness gave a lot of statements, testified in a lot of cases, and it's very important, all of this, for the Trial Chamber to be able to have an insight into all the things that this witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Conclude your cross-examination in an hour's time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in order to keep it short, I kindly ask you to reply with a "yes" or "no" wherever possible. Is it correct that in different statements you cited different number of times that were you taken out for work assignments while you were at the bunker?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but mostly it was not more than six times altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct -- excuse me, is it correct that you stated that you were taken out twice, four times, seven times?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: See, when we are talking about being taken out of prison, I talked about the more significant times that I was taken out. I went out of the bunker compound a number of times. But these six times, two, four, six times, that was when I was in some way exposed to firing from both sides of the separation line, and when I was doing some more difficult assignments that prisoners were taken out to carry out. And this was six times at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in one statement you said that you were never used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of human shields and what is a human shield is something that one cannot know unless they experience it. My escape from prison involved the classic use of human shields. However, when I went out to do certain work assignments, in a way I could also be considered as a human shield because the jobs that we were doing were in the areas between the two armies, in the areas of separation between the Serbian army and the Bosnian army. On the 5th of December, when I escaped from prison, I was in an actual human shield situation where I was exposed, in front of the Army of Republika Srpska, facing the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hides behind the grandfather in order to fire at the bear. Does that mean that you were placed in front of Serbian soldiers who were advancing and you were in the role of a human shield? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: The most significant human shield situation where I was -- where I was -- that I was in was on the 5th of December, when I escaped from the prison where I was kept captive. The Serbs placed us in front of them. We were carrying ammunition boxes, they placed heavy weapons on the shoulders of some prisoners and were pushing them in front of them. We were practically walking in front of them so that we would be exposed to Bosnia-Herzegovina army fire, and at the same time, in case we encountered an explosive or a device or a mine, we would be the first ones to trip or to be exposed to these explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were a live target or a human shield, is that the same thing to you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was a human shield, and at the same time, I served as a live target for the other side. We were used as a kind of shield behind which the Serbian army soldiers could hide because they held some of us by the shoulders and were pushing us in front of them. They also placed heavy weapons on our shoulders and they were walking in front, and before that, they were warned that they were not allowed to bend over, to try to seek cover in any way. They were instructed to behave like human live targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in which statement specifically did you describe that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever I was describing my escape. Wherever I said that I escaped, I said that I escaped from being a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will find that if we have time. Please tell us, you described that you were sent to cut trees, to do other things. What were the kinds of things that you did and is it correct that those who applied to go to work got more food and more cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are different forms of torture that people who were together in the camp with me were exposed to. Those who went out for work assignments, in order to be able to carry out these difficult tasks given to them, they were given certain quantities of food when they were doing these jobs. Not infrequently, those of us who stayed behind did not really get adequate quantities of food or were given that much attention from the Serbian soldiers. While prisoners were taken out for tasks outside of the compound, we were sent to cut wood, that's what I did specifically. We were sent for digging and covering up the trenches, whenever the lines moved forward, so mostly these were jobs involving trench digging between the line of separation between the two armies. This was when the Serbian army was moving its lines forward towards the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then they would release the prisoners into the area in front of them in order to dig the fortifications, in order that they could capture that area later. At one occasion I was taken out with a group of prisoners to the Ravne hill above Semizovac, this is a plateau that runs towards Ravne Nabozic mountain from Semizovac, and in mid-August, we were clearing the forest there, in order to create a clearing that was located between the two armies, and that forest was exposed to a fire the night before. It was torched. So besides being exposed to strong sunlight, we also suffered from the heat from the fire that raged in that area earlier. And at the same time, we had to clear the scorched trees in order to create a clearing, and at the time we were also suffering from a shortage of food and water. We were suffering from burns as well because we were not allowed to drag those smouldering pieces of wood but we actually had to pick them up and carry them to a place where that material was going to be burned. But those who were suffering from exhaustion, who couldn't work, who couldn't run, were subjected to physical torture. They were hit and they were struck by rifle butts, by the Serbian soldiers. One of the fingers on my left hand was hurt and then later when I returned to the camp, for days after that I didn't get proper medical treatment for that injury, so that the wound got infected and was treated only after I escaped from prison. This was after the 5th of December when I crossed over into the territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, you're making this big salad of lies here. Did the prisoners report voluntarily for work assignments?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some for which the detainees themselves reported. However, when it happened that in addition to agricultural work and trench digging, the prisoners were being used as human shields, then there were less and less volunteers. So in the beginning of September, hardly anyone wanted to volunteer for any kind of work because it was well known that they could be used as human shields as well. Or perhaps they could be exposed to gunfire in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, wherever possible, just say "yes" or "no." Did you report for work voluntarily ever and, if so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I never volunteered to go out to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was mistreated in the way that you described and was then beaten using rifle butts? Give us a name.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Suad Sosevic, Zahid Barucija and a few others who I cannot remember. I cannot remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that or did someone say that to you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Suad Sosevic at the Ravne hill above Semizovac, Zahid Barucija on the Zuci [phoen] plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was responsible for them, then? Who was it that escorted you up there, name and surname?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the name and surname of the person, the soldier, who was actually beating him. I didn't know his name. But the responsible person on that line, in this zone, rather, was Dragisa Damjanovic. So, at the time when he was mistreated, he was some kind of commander in the area. Dragisa Damjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many guards did you have in the bunker, Mr. Muracevic?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the number changed, it was, say, 15 or 20, but I cannot give you any definite figure as to how many there were. Around the bunker usually there would be about ten soldiers, ten guards, in different positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know the names of the persons who were taking you out to do that work?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the guards that were there -- well, we knew them but very often it wasn't the guards themselves who took people out to work, those who were guarding us at the place where we were held captive. Various persons came for this person, either members of military units or police structures or some local Serbs, and I was not aware of what they particularly did in that area. So it wasn't the guards who invariably escorted the prisoners to the locations where they worked, for which they were taken out of the place where they had been detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we cannot identify the Serb who mistreated these two men because they were so weak, right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that we cannot but I don't know. Specifically, Suad Sosevic was mistreated by Ranko Jankovic. He's the brother of a friend of mine from school, and he had some kind of a command position in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever you stated that before?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere, but I don't know whether it was included in the statements that are part of this sublimated statement. There are a lot of statements. There have been a lot of statements and I'm not sure that all of them are contained in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned some people who came from time to time and wore cockades, where?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually on their caps, berets, head gear, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that some persons mistreated others but they said that Branko Vlaco, the commander, should not find out about that. Was it your impression that they were afraid of Vlaco?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Vlaco was the commander of the prison, so the logic is that his subordinates were afraid if he were to find out what they did, especially if they did something that he did not tell them to do. However, sometimes some prison wardens and guards brought in persons who we did not know, or dogs, or they themselves took part in the mistreatment of prisoners, and on such occasions they would say to us that we could not convey that to Brano Vlaco, the commander of the prison. However, when certain mistreatments took place, when tear gas was brought into the bunker and things like that, in front of these guards and in front of Branko Vlaco, this kind of thing would happen but neither he nor the guards did anything particular to protect us. I am not sure that Branko Vlaco did not know what his subordinates were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, it would be a very good thing, and the Prosecution would appreciate it, if you would stick to the truth. This way, you are just ruining your very own credibility. And the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's not a comment that should be made by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that they were afraid of Branko Vlaco, and you even said in some statements that guards did not mistreat you but that some guards allowed unknown persons to enter the premises and mistreat people. On one occasion, when they threw some kind of gas in, the guards were trying to save people; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Muracevic, you want the reference for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had the amount of time that I had asked for, you'd have a reference too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state that, sir? That they were afraid that Branko Vlaco would find out what they did? That's one question, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: As for whether they were afraid or not, I do not remember having stated anywhere that they were afraid of this Branko Vlaco. However, as a person whose -- who was their boss in a way, if I can put it that way, they should be afraid if they did something without him knowing about it. However, when I said that in prison not all the guards were extremists who mistreated the camp inmates, that was presented in my statement, but some of them were more extreme and they themselves mistreated us who they were guarding, but at the same time they also brought in other people to mistreat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are wasting my time terribly. I just asked you whether they threatened you that the warden should not find out. In paragraph 11 of your statement, did you not say --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, Mr. Karadzic said that the witness said a certain thing. The witness said that he didn't say it and then he's telling him he's wasting his time. He's simply answering the allegation that's being put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not say in one statement in respect of persons who mistreated you, that they threatened you saying that the prison warden should not find out about that, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, that is just one situation in a sea of other situations in which they and the prison commander coordinated their intimidation of the detainees. Well, there was a certain situation when they took some money from a person who they brought into custody. And this person had collected that money in order to buy something for some other citizens. And then they threatened him saying that they -- that he should not tell the prison warden that they had taken that money from him. So that is that situation that you're getting at, whether they were afraid or not. Of course, they were afraid if they took something away from someone and did not report that to the prison administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And had they reported that, you say that they could get away with it, right, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC (Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, no one took that money away from me but they did take away this money from Asif Sehic. In the bunker we tried to resuscitate him for three days because he was beaten so badly. He said that when he came, the guards took some money away from him and threatened him that he should not report that to the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
